In my second year, Uday asked me to go with him to the college fest night. Not as a group. Just us. I said no so quickly that he looked hurt. I remember telling myself it was obvious: we'd have nothing to talk about, he'd realise I'm boring, and next week things would be weird in class. Better to keep things as they were.
I felt so clever that night. No awkward silences. No risk. I watched the fireworks from the hostel terrace with a packet of chips.
But the next year I noticed something. I'd said no to three more things the same way. A trip, a dance class, a friend's birthday in another city. Every no protected me from a bad evening that hadn't happened yet. And my weekends had got smaller and smaller.
Uday is married now. We still say hi. I still wonder.
— Disha

Today was swimming class number one. I didn't go in.
Papa signed me up at the colony pool because Salma goes there. When we reached, I looked at the blue water and my legs went wobbly. I told Papa, "It's too deep. It's dangerous. Somebody could drown." Nitin

subtype: Feeling guilty so must be guilty [Actor]
passage: In their dorm room in Toronto, Xin noticed that Mina had stopped coming to breakfast. She'd been quiet for a week, and she hadn't put up her fairy lights after the winter break. Xin's stomach knotted. The week before, Xin had cancelled their plan to go skating to study with another friend. That's it, Xin thought. I let her down. I made her sad. The guilt sat like a stone, and the stone felt like proof. Xin started bringing Mina muffins and apologising for small things: the noise, the good chair. Finally Mina said, "Why do you keep saying sorry?" Xin blurted out, "Because of the skating. I think I made you sad." Mina blinked. "Xin, I'm homesick. My grandmother's sick and I'm far away. It's not you." She paused. "But thank you for noticing." Xin sat down on the bed. The guilt had pointed at the wrong reason, but at the right person to care about.

qa.q: What had Xin cancelled the week before?
qa.a: Xin had cancelled their plan to go skating.

qa.q: Why did Xin keep apologising for small things?
qa.a: Xin felt guilty and was sure the cancelled skating plan had made Mina sad, treating that guilt as proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Xin now that Mina has explained?
qa.a: Keep caring for Mina, perhaps by staying company while she calls home, and suggest the dorm counsellor if the homesickness keeps weighing on her.

qa.q: What was it like for Mina to receive all those apologies?
qa.a: Mina was confused by the sorries, but grateful that someone noticed how low she was.

grounding: A student abroad feels guilty about a roommate's low mood and assumes the blame, while guilt proves only that Xin cares.

subtype: Feeling guilty so must be guilty [Actor]
passage: In the college library, Pradeep kept glancing at Tanuja across the table. Since Monday's group project meeting, she had barely spoken. On Monday he had said her section needed "a lot of work". Now she was sitting with headphones on and not even pretending to study. Pradeep felt a wave of guilt so heavy he couldn't read. I crushed her. She's miserable because of me. He wrote her a long apology on a page of his notebook and pushed it across. Tanuja read it and pulled off her headphones. "Pradeep, your comment was fair. I'm not upset about that." She hesitated. "My parents are separating. I found out on Sunday." Pradeep felt his face go hot. "I'm sorry. I thought it was me." "I know. You feel guilty about everything." She almost smiled. "Want to get chai? I don't want to be here." They walked out together, past the librarian's desk.

qa.q: What had Pradeep said about Tanuja's section on Monday?
qa.a: He had said her section needed "a lot of work".

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel so sure he had crushed Tanuja?
qa.a: Pradeep felt a heavy wave of guilt, and the strength of that feeling made it seem like proof that his comment caused her low mood.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do now to support Tanuja?
qa.a: Go for chai and listen, and gently mention the college counsellor if she wants someone to talk to about home.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel about Pradeep's long apology?
qa.a: Tanuja seemed a little amused by his guilt, and also glad to have someone to walk out with on a hard day.

grounding: A student sure his comment caused a friend's low mood learns guilt isn't evidence of wrongdoing, though it shows how much he values her.

passage: Reena, you asked how I got through my first board presentation. I'm Wasim, and honestly? I almost didn't. The night before, my chest was tight and my hands were cold. My brain said, "If you feel this bad, it's going to go badly." For years I'd believed that. Nervous meant doomed. So I did something my old mentor taught me. I said out loud to the mirror, "I feel anxious about the meeting. That is not the same as the meeting going badly." Then I looked at the facts. I'd practised four times. My numbers were checked. My manager had seen the slides. I let the nerves stay; I didn't fight them. I just didn't let them drive. The next morning my voice shook for the first two slides, and then it didn't. The board asked three questions. I answered all three. Nervous, yes. Doomed, no.

qa.q: How many times had Wasim practised before the board presentation?
qa.a: Wasim had practised four times.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel the night before, and what did the old belief say about it?
qa.a: Wasim felt anxious, with a tight chest and cold hands, and the old belief said feeling that bad meant the meeting would go badly.

qa.q: What made Wasim's approach work?
qa.a: Saying aloud that anxiety isn't the same as a bad meeting, checking the facts of the preparation, and letting the nerves stay without letting them steer.

qa.q: How might Reena use Wasim's story?
qa.a: Reena might feel reassured that nerves before a big moment are normal and try naming the feeling separately from the facts.

grounding: An adult tells a friend about separating feeling anxious about a board meeting from the meeting going badly and went ahead with the plan.

passage: I'm Binita, and I sit next to Madhav at the architecture firm. On the morning of his first solo client meeting, I noticed him at the coffee machine, tapping his cup and breathing slowly. He caught me watching and laughed. "My brain says I'm going to mess up because I feel sick," he said. "So I'm telling it: feeling nervous and the meeting going badly are two different things." He said it like he'd said it before. I don't know everything he was feeling, only what I could see: pale face, steady voice. Then he picked up his drawings and went in. Through the glass I saw him point at the model, answer questions, even laugh once. An hour later, he came out and dropped into the chair beside me. "Still nervous," he said. "And they signed off on phase one." I gave him a biscuit.

qa.q: What did the client sign off on?
qa.a: They signed off on phase one.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as Madhav went into the meeting?
qa.a: Binita seemed curious and quietly hopeful for Madhav, watching through the glass while not knowing everything he felt.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that helped him go ahead?
qa.a: He named the nerves and told himself they were different from the meeting going badly, then followed his plan and went in.

qa.q: What might the meeting have been like for Madhav?
qa.a: Madhav was nervous throughout, pale but steady, yet still able to point at the model and answer questions.

grounding: A colleague observes an adult tell himself that feeling nervous differs from a meeting going badly, and go ahead with the plan.

passage:
Sunday. Maria had a meeting with her new landlord on Tuesday about the broken water heater, and she already felt sick. She told Nandini, her flatmate, "It's going to go terribly. I can feel it." Nandini asked, "Is that a feeling or a fact?" Maria paused. "Feeling." They made a list of what she wanted to say: heater broken for two weeks, photos, request a repair date.
Tuesday. Before knocking on the landlord's door, Maria stood on the landing and said quietly, "I feel anxious. That doesn't mean it will go badly. I'll do the plan." Her voice wobbled, but she went through the list. The landlord looked at the photos and said a plumber would come Thursday.
Thursday. The plumber came. Maria stood in the hot shower for a long time. That night she told Nandini, "I was anxious the whole time. It still went fine." Nandini raised her mug. "Feelings are allowed. They just don't get to drive."

qa.q: When did the landlord say a plumber would come?
qa.a: The landlord said a plumber would come Thursday.

qa.q: How did Maria feel standing on the landing before the meeting?
qa.a: Maria felt anxious, with a wobbly voice, but chose to follow the plan anyway.

qa.q: What helped Maria separate the feeling from the outcome?
qa.a: Nandini's question, "Is that a feeling or a fact?", plus a clear list of points and the words she said to herself on the landing.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel hearing that the meeting went fine?
qa.a: Nandini seems pleased and warm, raising her mug, glad that Maria's anxiety didn't get to steer.

grounding: Over several days an adult treats her anxiety about a landlord meeting as a feeling, not a forecast, and follows her plan.

passage: The Johannesburg winter term was cold. She had a rule she never said out loud: I must always come first. I must never cry at school. When the maths results came back, she was second, behind Bao, by one mark. Her throat went tight. You must not cry, she told herself. You should have checked question four. She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt. At break, Bao came over, beaming. "We're both in the top two!" Lindiwe couldn't answer. She walked to the bathroom and cried, then felt even worse. Now she had broken two rules. On the bus home, her gran asked what was wrong. "I'm not first," she whispered. Gran said, "Who made that rule?" Lindiwe thought. Nobody had. "I did," she said.

qa.q: By how many marks was Lindiwe behind Bao?
qa.a: She was behind Bao by one mark.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe feel even worse after crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: She felt ashamed because she had now broken two of her own strict rules, always first and never cry.

qa.q: How could Lindiwe's gran help her further?
qa.a: Gran could help her soften the rules, for example to "I try my best" and "Crying is allowed", and notice when they make her feel worse.

qa.q: How might Bao see Lindiwe's silence at break?
qa.a: Bao was happy about them both being top two, so Lindiwe's silence might confuse or hurt Bao.

grounding: A girl holds herself to rules that she must always come first and never cry, and feels ashamed at a one-mark slip.

passage: In the last week of Ramzan, in the Class 6 science lab, Dilnaz was fasting, tired, and determined. She had rules for herself. I should always get full marks. I should never cry, even when I'm tired. When Sachin sir handed back the lab report, there was a 17 out of 20 in red. Dilnaz stared at it. Three marks. That's terrible. I should have done better. Her eyes stung and she blinked hard, angry at herself for even that. Sachin sir saw it. After class he said, "Dilnaz, 17 is a good mark. And you're fasting. What's the rule you're following?" "I should always get 20." "Who says?" She shrugged. "Me." "What happens when you miss it?" "I feel bad for days." He nodded. "That sounds like a heavy rule. What if it said, 'I'll try my best'?"

qa.q: What mark did Dilnaz get in the lab report?
qa.a: She got 17 out of 20.

qa.q: Why were Dilnaz's eyes stinging over three missed marks?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt ashamed and angry at herself, because her rule said she should always get full marks and never cry.

qa.q: How did Sachin sir help Dilnaz?
qa.a: He asked about the rule she was following and what it cost her, then suggested a gentler one: "I'll try my best."

qa.q: How might Sachin sir see Dilnaz's 17 out of 20?
qa.a: He sees it as a good mark, especially while fasting, and seems concerned about how harsh she is on herself.

grounding: During Ramzan a girl who tells herself she must always score full marks and never cry feels ashamed at a small slip, and a teacher questions the rule.

passage:
Navratri, day one. Indu told herself she must win the colony drawing contest like last year. She stayed up late colouring. Her little sister Sabina asked her to come and dance garba. "No. I must practise. I should be the best."
Day four. The results were out. Indu came third. She went home and hid in the cupboard. She was not supposed to cry. Crying was for babies. But she did. Then she felt worse for crying.
Day nine. Sabina came and sat with her while she was drawing again. "Why are you always sad when you're not first?" Indu said, "Because I should be." "Says who?" Indu thought. "I don't know." Sabina pulled her to the garba circle. Indu danced, messily. She didn't win anything. She laughed anyway, and for the first time that festival, she didn't feel bad.

qa.q: What place did Indu get in the colony drawing contest?
qa.a: Indu came third.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel worse after crying in the cupboard?
qa.a: Indu felt ashamed, because her rule said she should never cry, so breaking it added guilt to the sadness.

qa.q: What helped Indu ease up by day nine?
qa.a: Sabina asked who made the rule, and pulled her into garba, where she could enjoy something without needing to be first.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Indu refused to dance on day one?
qa.a: Sabina may have felt disappointed and puzzled that her sister chose practice over fun.

grounding: Across Navratri a girl tells herself she must always win and never cry, feels ashamed at a slip, and slowly loosens the rule.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, by Chinmay
Sarita came to see me today, very angry. Her parents had booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday. "They should know it matters to me. I shouldn't have to tell them." I asked if she had told them. She said, "They should just know." Then she talked about her friends. Two of them couldn't come to her dance show last month. "Real friends make time for things like that. Always." She has been silent at home for three days.
I asked, "What happens when people don't do what they should?" She said, "I get angry and stop talking to them." "Does that get you what you want?" She was quiet.
What I did next: we practised one sentence she could say to her parents tonight: "This birthday matters to me. Can we talk about the dates?"

qa.q: What did Sarita's parents book?
qa.a: They booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday.

qa.q: Why is Sarita so angry at her parents and friends?
qa.a: Sarita feels resentful because she believes they should understand and always be free without being told, and they fell short.

qa.q: What practical step did Chinmay offer?
qa.a: Chinmay helped Sarita practise one clear sentence to say to her parents tonight, so she could ask instead of expecting them to know.

qa.q: How might Sarita's parents see the three days of silence?
qa.a: They are probably confused and worried, not knowing that the birthday matters so much to her.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager who thinks parents should understand without being told and friends should always be free, and whose resentment grows faster than talk.

passage:
Saturday night
I'm so angry with Leela. I told her last week I had my first football match today. She should have known I'd want her there. Best friends should come without being asked. She went to her cousin's engagement instead. Didn't even message "good luck".
And Mummy. She should have known I'd be starving after the match. But she was at Nani's and there was only cold rice.
Everyone is always letting me down. Why do I have to spell everything out? People who care should just KNOW.
I haven't replied to Leela's "how was the match??" message. It's been four hours.
Actually, diary, reading this back, I never asked Leela to come. I said, "I have a match Saturday." That's not the same as "Please come." And I never told Mummy what time I'd be home.
Hmm. Maybe I'll reply to Leela.
Divyansh

qa.q: What did Divyansh tell Leela last week?
qa.a: Divyansh told Leela about the first football match on Saturday.

qa.q: What is Divyansh feeling about Leela and Mummy, and why?
qa.a: Divyansh feels resentful and let down, believing people who care should know what Divyansh needs without being told.

qa.q: What did Divyansh notice that could help next time?
qa.a: That saying "I have a match" is not the same as asking "Please come", so asking clearly could prevent the anger.

qa.q: How might Leela see the four hours of silence after her message?
qa.a: Leela might feel confused or worried, since she asked how the match went and got no reply.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows expecting a friend and a parent to understand needs without being told, and resentment building faster than conversation.
